Simulate a power series with a given average and normalised power

Source: R/simulate.r
simulate_power.Rd

Inverts the metrics: rather than summarising a ride you rode, it builds a second-by-second series that would produce the numbers you name.

Usage

simulate_power(n_seconds, target_ap, target_np, smoothness = 0.98)

Arguments

n_seconds

Number of seconds to simulate.

target_ap

Average power to hit, in watts.

target_np

Normalised power to hit, in watts. Cannot be below target_ap.

smoothness

Autocorrelation of the underlying effort, between 0 and 1. Higher values give long sustained efforts, lower values a more punchy ride. At a given normalised power this changes the character of the session, not its statistics.

Value

Numeric vector of per-second power values, hitting both targets exactly. Values are not rounded to whole watts, which would perturb them.

Details

The problem is wildly underdetermined — thousands of seconds, two constraints — so the shape has to come from somewhere. Here it comes from an autocorrelated process, which is what riding looks like: you hold a power for minutes at a time rather than jumping about at random. Normalised power is defined on a thirty-second rolling mean, and second-by-second noise averages away inside that window, so a series of independent draws has a variability index of 1 no matter how wide its spread and noise alone cannot produce a normalised power above the average.

Scale and shape are then solved separately, which is what makes both targets exact. Both metrics scale linearly with power, so their ratio does not depend on the overall level: raising the series to a power sets the variability index, and multiplying through afterwards sets the average without disturbing it. That leaves one monotone equation in one unknown rather than a search over every second of the ride.

Feasibility

Nothing here knows about critical power, so nothing stops you naming targets no rider could hold. A normalised power above threshold sustained for an hour comes back as a series that would exhaust any W' several times over, and that is the target being impossible rather than the simulation being wrong: a steady hour at that power would fail the same test. Check the intensity you are asking for before reading anything into the shape that comes back.

Within a feasible intensity the shape holds up, but its upper tail is lognormal and widens with the variability index, so a ragged ride posts sustained peaks — the best thirty seconds, not the peak second — beyond what the same ride's five-minute best implies. At a high variability index the series stops being a plausible ride and is only a series with the right two numbers.

Examples

ride <- withr::with_seed(1, simulate_power(3600, target_ap = 180, target_np = 220))
c(average_power(ride), normalised_power(ride))
#> [1] 180 220
